title: Frontend tests: components and services
goal: Test the Angular side of ApplyTrack: stores, services, guards and key components.

concepts: Angular testing with TestBed (Vitest or Karma/Jasmine, whichever your CLI set up)
Testing services with provideHttpClientTesting and HttpTestingController
Testing stores: computed values and state after actions
Testing guards and interceptors as plain functions
Component tests: render, interact, assert on the DOM (Angular Testing Library is optional)
What not to test: framework internals and styling details

build.task: In applytrack/web, write 20+ tests: ApplicationsApi (correct URLs, query params and bodies via HttpTestingController); ApplicationsStore (loading/error states, optimistic status change and rollback); AuthService (login stores token, logout clears it, restoreSession); authGuard (redirects with returnUrl); authInterceptor (adds the header only for /api); StatusBadge (right label and class per status); ApplicationForm (validation messages, submit disabled when invalid, edit mode pre-fills). Add the tests to the README and a root npm test that runs api and web tests.
acceptance: 20+ frontend tests pass
HTTP tested with HttpTestingController (no real network)
Optimistic update rollback has a test
Guard and interceptor tested
One root command runs all api and web tests

hints: TestBed.configureTestingModule({ providers: [provideHttpClient(), provideHttpClientTesting()] }); const http = TestBed.inject(HttpTestingController); ... const req = http.expectOne(r => r.url === '/api/applications'); req.flush({ data: [], meta: {...} });
Test guards with TestBed.runInInjectionContext(() => authGuard(route, state)).
For the rollback test, make the request fail with req.flush('x', { status: 500, statusText: 'Server Error' }) and assert the status went back.

explainBack.q: What does HttpTestingController let you check?
lookFor: which requests were made (URL, method, body)
respond with fake data or errors

explainBack.q: Which frontend test catches the most important bug, and why?

lastHintExplanation: HttpTestingController captures requests instead of sending them: you assert the URL, method and body, then answer with whatever data or error the test needs. That makes rollback and error paths, which are hard to trigger by hand, easy to test, and http.verify() fails the test if anything unexpected was requested.

dsa.note: New pattern. Ways(n) = ways(n−1) + ways(n−2). Write the recursion first, add memoisation, then a loop with two variables.

title: End-to-end tests with Playwright
goal: Automate the most important user journeys in a real browser.

concepts: End-to-end tests: the whole stack, through the browser
Playwright: test, page, locators by role and label, expect with auto-waiting
Starting the API and web app for tests (webServer config)
Seeding and cleaning test data through the API
Keep E2E tests few and focused on critical journeys
Trace viewer for debugging failures

build.task: In applytrack: add Playwright (e2e/ folder) with webServer starting the API (against the test database) and the web app. Write 5 journeys: (1) register → land on the dashboard; (2) add an application → it appears in the list; (3) change its status on the board using the keyboard 'Move to…' menu → dashboard counts update; (4) edit and delete with the confirmation dialog; (5) logged-out user visiting /applications is redirected to login and returns after logging in. Use getByRole and getByLabel locators only. Each test creates its own user. Record a trace on failure and add an npm run e2e script.
acceptance: 5 E2E journeys pass headless
Only role/label/text locators (no CSS class selectors)
Tests are independent (each creates its own user)
One command starts the servers and runs the tests
Trace is recorded on failure

hints: Create a unique user per test: const email = `e2e+${Date.now()}@example.com`; register through the UI in the first test and through the API (request fixture) in the others to save time.
Locators: page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add application' }), page.getByLabel('Company'). If a locator is hard to write, your markup probably lacks a label, which is an accessibility bug too.
playwright.config.ts: use: { trace: 'retain-on-failure' }; open it with npx playwright show-trace.
proof: Commit with the e2e folder and config.

explainBack.q: Why use getByRole and getByLabel instead of CSS selectors?

lastHintExplanation: Role and label locators find elements the way users (and screen readers) do, so tests survive class-name changes and fail when accessibility breaks. E2E tests are slow and more brittle, so keep them for the journeys that must never break and let unit and API tests cover the details.

concepts: A portfolio README: hook, screenshot/GIF, live link, features, tech stack, architecture, setup, tests
Architecture diagram (Mermaid or Excalidraw)
Architecture Decision Records (ADRs): context, decision, consequences
.env.example with every variable explained
Writing for two readers: recruiters skim, engineers dig

build.task: In applytrack: rewrite the root README: a one-line pitch, a GIF of the board and dashboard, a 'Live demo' link (placeholder until Day 131) with demo credentials, features, tech stack with why each was chosen, a Mermaid architecture diagram (browser → Angular → API → PostgreSQL, plus auth flow), setup steps for local development, how to run each kind of test, and project structure. Mermaid diagram renders on GitHub

Setup steps tested from a fresh clone

hints: Record a GIF with ScreenToGif (Windows), Kap (macOS) or Peek (Linux). Keep it under 10 seconds and 5 MB.

ADR format: # 2. Store JWT in localStorage
## Context
## Decision
## Consequences (good and bad)
Put the most impressive thing (the GIF) above the fold. Recruiters often look for under a minute.
proof: Link to the README on GitHub.

explainBack.q: Summarise one of your ADRs: what did you decide, and what did you give up?
What does a recruiter see in the first 10 seconds of your README?

lastHintExplanation: ADRs show interviewers that you make deliberate choices and understand their costs, which is exactly what they probe in project discussions. A README that leads with a pitch, a GIF and a live link respects a recruiter's 30 seconds, while the setup and architecture sections serve engineers who dig deeper.

title: Docker: containerising the API and web app
goal: Package ApplyTrack into containers so it runs the same everywhere.

concepts: Images vs containers; layers and caching
Multi-stage builds: build with dev dependencies, run with production ones only
.dockerignore (node_modules, .env, dist, .git)
Serving the Angular build with Nginx (with SPA fallback to index.html)
docker compose: api + web + postgres with a volume and healthchecks
Binding to 0.0.0.0 inside containers; non-root user

build.task: In applytrack: write api/Dockerfile (multi-stage: build TypeScript, then a slim runtime with npm ci --omit=dev, non-root user, CMD node dist/index.js), web/Dockerfile (build Angular, serve with nginx:alpine using an nginx.conf with try_files $uri /index.html and /api proxied to the api service), .dockerignore files, and docker-compose.yml with postgres (named volume, healthcheck), api (depends_on postgres healthy, runs migrations on start) and web. docker compose up should give a working app at http://localhost:8080. Record image sizes before and after the multi-stage build in docs/docker.md.
acceptance: docker compose up starts all three services; the app works at localhost:8080
Multi-stage builds; runtime images contain no dev dependencies or source TypeScript
.dockerignore excludes node_modules, .env, dist and .git
Deep-link reloads work through Nginx
Data survives docker compose down and up (named volume)
docs/docker.md records image sizes and explains each Dockerfile line

hints: Copy package*.json and run npm ci BEFORE copying the source: Docker caches that layer, so rebuilds after code changes skip reinstalling.
nginx.conf: location /api/ { proxy_pass http://api:4000; } location / { try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html; }. Inside compose, services reach each other by service name.
Healthcheck for postgres: test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres"], and in api: depends_on: postgres: condition: service_healthy.
proof: Commit with Dockerfiles, compose file and docs/docker.md.

explainBack.q: Why copy package.json and install before copying the rest of the source?
What does a multi-stage build give you?
lookFor: no build tools/dev deps in production

lastHintExplanation: Docker caches each layer and reuses it until its inputs change. Installing dependencies from package*.json before copying your source means code changes don't trigger a full reinstall. Multi-stage builds compile in a full image, then copy only the output into a slim runtime image, which is smaller, faster to deploy and has fewer tools for an attacker.

predict.q: Inside a container, the API listens on 127.0.0.1:4000 and you run docker run -p 4000:4000. Can your browser reach it?
options: No: it only accepts connections from inside the container
predict.why: 127.0.0.1 inside the container is the container itself; bind to 0.0.0.0.

title: Deploying on Coolify
goal: Put ApplyTrack on the internet with HTTPS, a real database and automatic deploys.

concepts: Coolify: a self-hosted, open-source platform (a free alternative to Heroku/Render) running on a VPS
Deploying from a GitHub repo with Docker Compose or Dockerfiles
Managed PostgreSQL in Coolify; backups
Environment variables and secrets in the platform, not in git
Domains, DNS records and automatic HTTPS (Let's Encrypt)
Deploy on push (webhooks) and reading deployment logs

build.task: Deploy ApplyTrack. Options: Coolify on a cheap VPS (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, or an Oracle Cloud free-tier VM), or if you can't use a VPS, a free tier of Render/Railway/Fly for the API plus Neon or Supabase for PostgreSQL and any static host for the web app. Configure all environment variables in the platform (a new strong JWT_SECRET, CORS_ORIGINS set to your real domain, NODE_ENV=production), run migrations, seed a demo account (demo@applytrack.dev / a password shown in the README), enable HTTPS, set trust proxy, and turn on deploy-on-push. Write docs/deployment.md with every step and the problems you hit.
acceptance: App is live over HTTPS on a public URL
Demo account works and is listed in the README
No secrets in git; production uses its own JWT_SECRET
Pushing to main triggers a redeploy
/health and /ready work in production
docs/deployment.md is a complete, repeatable guide

hints: Most first deploys fail on environment variables. Read the deployment logs first; your config validation should tell you exactly what's missing.
CORS in production: if the web app and API share a domain via the Nginx proxy (/api), you may not need CORS at all. That's simpler and safer.
Behind Coolify's proxy, app.set('trust proxy', 1) is needed for correct client IPs in rate limiting and logs.

explainBack.q: Walk through what happens between git push and the new version being live.
What was the hardest deployment problem and how did you debug it?

lastHintExplanation: On push, a webhook tells the platform to pull the commit, build the images, start the new containers, check their health and switch traffic to them, while the reverse proxy terminates HTTPS with a Let's Encrypt certificate. When it fails, the build and runtime logs, plus your startup config validation, are where the answer is.

title: Debug lab: the container that won't answer, and production checks
goal: Fix common Docker mistakes, then run a production checklist on your live app.

concepts: Binding to localhost inside a container
Ignoring PORT from the environment
Running dev servers and dev dependencies in production images
Leaking .env and local node_modules into images without .dockerignore
A production checklist: HTTPS, headers, errors, logs, backups, monitoring

build.task: Part 1: copy the starter into day132-debug/ in node-playground, run npm install once (to create package-lock.json), then docker compose up --build. Expected: curl http://localhost:8080/health returns { status: 'ok', env: 'production' }; the log says 'listening on 4000'; docker compose exec api ls -a shows no .env file; the container runs node server.js (not nodemon) and has no devDependencies installed. There are 4 bugs; fix each in its own commit. Part 2: on your live ApplyTrack, run Mozilla Observatory and Lighthouse, test a 500 error (no stack trace leaks), check logs are visible in the platform, set up a daily database backup and a free uptime monitor (e.g. UptimeRobot) on /health. Record everything in docs/production-checklist.md. Write week22-notes.md.

Image runs node server.js with production dependencies only (npm ci --omit=dev)

hints: curl gets 'connection reset' or 'empty reply'. Inside the container, run docker compose exec api wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:3000/health: it works there. Which address is the server listening on, and which port?
Run docker compose exec api ls -a. Why are .env and node_modules from your laptop in there? What file tells Docker what not to send in the build context?
docker compose exec api ps shows nodemon. Production images should install with npm ci --omit=dev and start with node server.js.
proof: Link to your last fix commit and your production checklist.

lookFor: CMD dev + dev deps → npm ci --omit=dev and node server.js

explainBack.q: Why is a .env file inside an image a security problem even if you never publish the image?
lookFor: anyone with the image can read the secret
layers keep files even if deleted later

lastHintExplanation: 1) Listening on 127.0.0.1 only accepts connections from inside the container; bind to 0.0.0.0. 2) The port is hard-coded to 3000, but compose maps 8080 to 4000; use process.env.PORT. 3) With no .dockerignore, COPY . . puts your .env and macOS node_modules into the image; add .dockerignore and copy package files first. 4) npm run dev runs nodemon with dev dependencies; use npm ci --omit=dev and CMD ["node", "server.js"].

predict.q: A Dockerfile copies .env, then a later layer runs RUN rm .env. Is the secret gone from the image?
options: No, it's still in the earlier layer
Only if the image is pushed
predict.why: Layers are additive; the file remains in the layer that added it.
